html:
In-ear monitors (IEMs) are a monitoring system used in live performance. Through earphones, singers and instrumentalists hear a mix of themselves and their accompaniment, which helps them keep their timing and pitch more precisely.

Origins and development

The story begins in the late 1950s, when pocket transistor radios appeared, equipped with the first portable earphones. Remarkably, in 1965 a 13-year-old named Stephen Ambrose made sealed monitoring earpieces out of clay, a pioneer of the first generation of in-ear monitors. In 1979 Sony launched the Walkman, bringing stereo headphones to the masses and encouraging the idea of replacing stage wedges with headphone monitoring. True IEM technology arrived in the mid-1980s, when the British sound engineer Chrys Lindop developed a wireless in-ear system for star artists such as Stevie Wonder, so that singers could hear their own voices in real time during concerts. In 1987 Lindop and his colleagues launched the first commercial IEM system, the “Radio Station,” and many major tours began to adopt it. In the 1990s Marty Garcia, founder of the American company Future Sonics, introduced custom in-ear monitors, building personalized earpieces from Walkman drivers and the artists’ ear impressions. In the early 2000s, manufacturers such as Westone, Sensaphonics and Shure released multi-driver IEMs and adopted digital wireless transmission, further improving sound quality and reliability. Today in-ear monitoring is standard equipment for professional performers and makes live performance far easier.

Stage monitoring before IEMs

Before in-ear monitors, musicians relied mainly on floor wedges at the front of the stage to hear themselves. These loudspeakers faced the performers, with their backs to the audience, so singers and players heard themselves from in front. But as stage volume rose, wedges struggled to deliver a clear sound and easily caused echoes on stage and microphone feedback (howling). They were also bulky and fixed in place, so a musician who moved away from them could no longer hear the music. To hear themselves, singers often had to stay in the so-called sweet spot and get used to the delay of sound reflected around the room. Venues were noisy, and the band and vocals bouncing back from the auditorium reached the singer’s ears late, tempting them to drag, which could easily throw off their accuracy.

Performing in the IEM era

With IEMs, singers can wear custom earpieces and hear their personal mix directly through a wireless receiver. However loud the stage, they can still hear their own voice in real time. Stage volume drops sharply as a result, reducing the risk of feedback and protecting hearing. Each performer can also set their own monitor level, turning up the elements that matter most to them without affecting anyone else. In short, concerts in the IEM era are more precise and more flexible, and singers can roam the stage or face the audience without losing their monitor signal.

With and without IEMs: a comparison

  • Monitoring: before IEMs, performers depended on large stage speakers, with a muddy sound and frequent feedback; with IEMs, each performer monitors through earphones, with a clear sound and isolation from outside noise.

  • Delay: traditional monitoring often suffered from delay and distortion; with IEMs, singers hear their voice almost in real time, which reduces timing errors caused by delay.

  • Control: with IEMs, everyone has an independent monitor mix and can adjust the balance of what they want to hear; without them, everyone hears the same mix sent out by the engineer.

  • Stage layout: without IEMs, heavy monitor speakers clutter the stage; with IEMs, the stage is clean and musicians can move more freely.

  • Hearing protection: IEMs significantly lower stage sound pressure levels and reduce damage to hearing; traditional monitoring often needs high levels to be heard, which can do harm over years of performing.

Overall, IEM technology has greatly improved both the quality of performances and the experience of singers, and it is now an indispensable part of the modern concert.

Key milestones

  • 1954 – The first commercial transistor radio goes on sale, with an early form of portable earphone.

  • 1979 – Sony launches the Walkman; stereo earphones become widespread, laying the groundwork for the idea of stage IEMs.

  • Mid-1980s – Chrys Lindop develops wireless in-ear monitoring for Stevie Wonder and other artists, and IEMs begin to appear at concerts.

  • 1987 – The first commercial IEM system, the “Radio Station,” comes to market and is adopted by Rod Stewart, Peter Gabriel and others.

  • 1993 – Future Sonics in the US introduces custom IEMs, combining Walkman earphone drivers with artists’ ear impressions.

  • 2000s – Several audio manufacturers introduce IEMs with multiple drivers and digital wireless technology, and IEMs mature and become widespread.

  • 2010s to today – IEM technology keeps improving, with features such as active noise cancellation and adjustable ambient sound, and IEMs are used ever more widely in performance and personal listening.
